claims.text: Post-sintering HIP will close residual pores in partially consolidated W–Cu composites.
Post-sintering HIP will improve W–Cu interfacial bonding.
Post-sintering HIP will increase the bulk density of W–Cu composites relative to SPS-only or infiltration-only baselines.
Post-sintering HIP will improve the mechanical performance of W–Cu composites relative to SPS-only or infiltration-only baselines.
Post-sintering HIP will improve the thermal performance of W–Cu composites relative to SPS-only or infiltration-only baselines.
Mechanical alloying and spark-plasma sintering can be used in powder-based fabrication and consolidation routes.
W–Cu compacts produced by mechanical alloying, infiltration, or SPS can retain residual porosity and imperfect W–Cu interfaces.
A post-consolidation HIP cycle at 1100–1200 °C and at least 100 MPa is suitable for densifying W–Cu composites.
Encapsulation and treatment in an inert or vacuum environment for sufficient time will promote W–Cu densification.
High temperature and isostatic pressure reduce porosity and improve interface cohesion in W–Cu.
Elevated temperature and uniform pressure facilitate interdiffusion at W–Cu boundaries.
Elevated temperature and uniform pressure facilitate plastic flow and pore collapse at W–Cu boundaries.
The proposed interdiffusion, plastic flow, and pore collapse produce a denser microstructure with greater load-bearing capacity.
SPS-only and infiltration-only W–Cu composites often exhibit incomplete densification and voids that impair strength and thermal transport.
HIP may increase W–Cu composite density by up to several percent.
The intervention is likely effective for W–Cu composites both with and without minor alloying additions.
The intervention is likely effective at sample sizes typical of fusion-reactor joints, while very large or non-standard architectures require industrial-scale verification.
The direction of the predicted density and property improvements is qualitatively supported by prior literature.
Direct literature comparisons between HIP-treated and non-HIP W–Cu are limited.
